newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Thai currency controls seen positive but risky.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thai currency controls seen positive but risky.

text.p: Thailand's central bank said on Wednesday that it would soon formalise currency controls imposed since last month to repel baht predators, but analysts believed the move could be a double-edged sword.

The plan was seen as positive because it would curb baht speculation at a delicate time for the economy. But was also considered risky because it could restrict foreign fund inflows needed to finance a wide current account deficit.
"We are working on permanent measures which will institutionalise existing controls and more," a senior Bank of Thailand official told Reuters.
Analysts were mostly receptive to the move, but cautioned that it could strongly backfire on Thailand, a net importer of capital, if the measures were poorly executed.
"I see this as good news for Thailand because the country is not ready to open its floodgates to speculators," said an analyst at a major U.S. investment bank who declined to be identified.
"Without proper exchange controls, you cannot insulate your economy from foreign speculators and conduct independent monetary policy," he said.

"So if exchange controls are applied selectively, they will be good for the country. Many countries in the region have capital controls and yet they don't have problems. Why should Thailand have problems?" he said.
Samarjit Shankar, BZW chief economist for Asia-Pacific, agreed that the controls could reduce the Thai currency's volatility but could at the same time affect capital inflows.

"It could introduce degrees of hesitation in future capital inflows into Thailand...It could also indirectly increase the risk premiums in investing in Thailand because the capital is no longer freely convertible," he said.

The central bank launched the controls in mid-May, cutting off supplies of baht from local sources to speculative foreign investors, forcing them to borrow in baht to cover short positions at extremely high interest rates.
The move was an attempt to strike back at speculators who have swooped on the embattled currency since late last year.
This week, the central bank plugged yet another loophole by restricting the baht from leaving the country following sales of Thai stocks by foreign investors.
The senior Bank of Thailand official stressed that the measures would not affect capital flows intended as genuine investment.
"We aim to keep a tight rein on the currency. Genuine capital flows for investment will not be affected. We are only clamping down on speculators in the baht with these measures," he said.

The Thai baht surged against the dollar to a new 13-year high in offshore markets following the central bank statement that it would formalise a two-tier baht market -- one offshore and the other onshore, dealers said.
By late afternoon, the baht had rallied to 23.730/23.830 to the dollar in offshore markets from 24.000/24.100 in the early morning. The baht was steady at 25.675/25.695 in the domestic market.

Sporadic attacks on the baht have made it difficult for the Bank of Thailand's interest rate policy, forcing the central bank to keep rates high to fend off speculation despite the nation's worst economic slump in a decade.
Other analysts cautioned the central bank to be selective in its choice of capital controls.
Jimmy Koh of Singapore-based research house I.D.E.A. doubted the two-tier market would work and suggested the central bank opt for Singapore-style capital controls.
Singapore requires financial institutions to notify monetary authorities before lending any amount above S$5.0 million ($3.5 million) to non-residents.

"The controls will no doubt flush out speculators from the market and make it more stable. However, the Bank of Thailand will have to be careful and selective on the kinds of controls it will use," he said.

Koh said a two-tier baht market made a lot of genuine investors uncomfortable. "The Thai baht is mostly traded outside Thailand and the hedging is done out of the forward market where the liquidity is low and the cost is high," he said.
